beats.trigger: does organisational mess still matter too much?

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: Nothing new. The same promise as the Big Idea, said again.

beats.trigger: You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: I can't review everything my fourteen people and their agents produce, so the standard has to be written down.

beats.trigger: measured judgment, made runnable
beats.got: Last module's scored benchmark ended up as a judge file I can re-run.

beats.trigger: every number traces to a file
beats.got: That is exactly the test my CFO would apply. No invented names, and every number traces to a source.

beats.trigger: A grounded mail can still be useless, so you need both.
beats.got: A mail that is true but forgettable is its own failure, so a second check should ask whether the reader will act.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: The judge stays fixed and the generator's tactic file gets rewritten. The improvement lives in a file, not in my prompts.

beats.trigger: You decide which details the system must never miss.
beats.got: The eval has to check what matters, where a mistake would cost something. It's a bit abstract.

beats.trigger: A yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick.
beats.got: The plan is to write a tactic, run the judge once, then let the lead agent loop three or more rounds with helpers.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: Run the judge by hand once so I know what it catches before the loop runs.

beats.trigger: Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: The loop runs on its own. The parallel-search and model-training side questions are fine but not my topic.

beats.trigger: Failed numbers in round 3 mean the tactic cannot handle numbers yet; weak claims marked grounded mean the judge has a blind spot.
beats.got: The notes tell me whether the generator or the judge is the weak part, and the SHA check shows whether the judge moved.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Each round's feedback went into the tactic file without me. I'd still like to see the diffs.

beats.trigger: You do not inspect every output; you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: My job moves from fixing outputs to owning the standard. Plan, do, check, act, with the improvement kept on disk for the next run.

beats.trigger: Take-home: put any judge in a loop that improves the thing it scores.
beats.got: I can wrap any judge, for example one on my pricing brief, in the same loop.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: Flagged claims hit zero, but that only means the judge has nothing left to find.

beats.trigger: A grounded claim can still be vague or obvious, and this judge passes it.
beats.got: A flat score tells me about the judge's limits, not about the work. That is where my own judgment has to come back in.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: I should score a handful of outputs by hand and compare them to the judge before I trust it. It's an afternoon, once per judge.

beats.trigger: The rest is yours to name.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.

take_homes: The improvement lives in a tactic file on disk, rewritten each round by a judge that stays fixed. Better prompts aren't where it happens.
A grounded output still isn't a good one. I need a second check for whether the reader will act, and a flat score only means the judge has run out of things to flag.
I check the judge once by hand against a few outputs, and I keep reading real outputs myself on a calendar date.

monday.move: Take the pilot-cohort pricing brief, write a short generation tactic and a groundedness judge for it, run three rounds, and check that the judge file's SHA is unchanged. Then score five briefs by hand against the judge.
monday.who: Me, then show the result to two people on the pricing working group
monday.when: Monday morning for the setup, with the loop running while I'm in meetings
monday.stop_condition: Flagged claims stop dropping, or the judge passes something I'd have sent back
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context and judge files, so everyone keeps their own copy and this stays a personal experiment

misconception.why: The gain came from a rewritten tactic file under a fixed judge, not from me wording prompts better. I still think good prompts matter for the first draft of the tactic, so I'm not fully convinced.

one_line: Good on how to make a loop trustworthy: fix the judge and check it by hand. The second half repeats itself, and I still don't know how my team shares any of it.
